title: Understanding the Jesus Journey Survey
html:
Where From Here?

  • Please note: by Spring 2018, a comprehensive set of Journey Survey debriefing materials will be available in a variety of formats that will include written guidance and videos (including live debriefing sessions). This material will be automatically made available to everyone who has previously purchased the Jesus Journey survey.
  • Realizing that most small churches cannot afford to hire a consultant who will facilitate an effective debriefing process, we are committed to constructing effective materials that will make understanding and utilizing their Journey survey reports a reachable goal for every church, regardless of size or budget.
  • Our initial guidance is provided here in text form. As soon as possible, we will work on more effective ways of communicating what we have observed and learned as to how churches can best interpret and use the information that can be gleaned from the Jesus Journey survey reports.

Journey Survey Structure

Belief, Experience and Behavior:

  • Of course, to become like Jesus must mean more than simply altering behavior. Jesus made it clear that his work of transformation would progress from the inside out: a new heart with new motivations would generate new ways of behaving. Nothing less would result in the New Creation that God was intending.
  • For this reason our Journey survey looks at our spiritual journey as a three-stranded cord. It first of all examines the interplay between three factors:
    • Our understanding and embrace of Jesus’ teaching about his Father and Jesus’ central message: the Kingdom of God.
    • Our experience of life with God and how it affects us from the inside out, reflecting our life with Jesus to others.
    • Our actions and the degree to which our behaviors communicate God’s love and truth and welcome God’s presence and power.
  • Because the way we live our lives is an outgrowth of these three realities joining together, our survey reports look at our journey through the lens of four different goal areas — ways in which we aspire to become more like Jesus (see the church report for a summary of these Journey Goals).
  • Each goal is then broken further into four “pathways” — ways of walking toward Jesus such as communicating with God, expressing God’s love, and stewarding God’s resources, etc. (More detailed information is given in the church report.)

Guiding Principles

Becoming Like Jesus is a Journey:

  • The early Christians were called “Followers of the Way,” an expression which continues to define our faith. Saying “yes” to the invitation of Jesus is not a contractual event; it is the beginning of a journey. The Christian life is an adventure of discovery: a life-long realization of what life can be when lived fully with God as opposed to without him. This is a journey in which we must be fully engaged. Imitating Jesus and becoming like him fully depends upon our cooperation with the grace he willingly extends toward us.

Starting, not stopping, conversation is the primary goal of the survey:

  • Actually taking the survey is not the end point of the Jesus Journey process; it is only the beginning of a fruitful season of discussion and discovery.
  • The results from this survey are not designed to lead straight into “solutions.” The purpose of this evaluation is to catalyze rich conversation, not to preclude it. Evaluation always creates the opportunity for fruitful interaction in that it creates readiness to consider change. This openness can be an important key to enable us to start asking better questions and exploring pathways toward new goals.

Invitation:

  • “For I know the plans I have for you,” declares the Lord, “plans to prosper you and not to harm you, plans to give you hope and a future.” (Jeremiah 29:11, NIV)
  • God’s posture toward us is always one of invitation. As demonstrated through the prophecy given through Jeremiah above, even when separation from God has resulted in destructive consequences, God’s ultimate plan and intention is for restoration, blessing and growth.
  • Personal evaluation is seen as a good thing in Scripture. “Search me, God, and know my heart; test me and know my anxious thoughts. See if there is any offensive way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting.” (Psalm 139:23–24, NIV) This Psalm, ascribed to David, expresses the confidence that becoming aware of the real state of our outer behavior and inner motivation is to be welcomed and not feared. It is a key to partnering with God’s invitation to us.
  • Knowing where we are along our path means we will know how and where to call out to God for his grace and empowering so that we can break free and move ahead. Additionally, seeing what God has already done in us encourages our hearts to re-engage with him for what lies ahead for us yet. While we never fully arrive in this life, as we trust God’s process and plans for us, we become more and more fully alive.

A snapshot, not a movie:

  • What this survey can do is give you and your community a picture of where you are right now in your walks together with Jesus. What it cannot do is convey the degree to which there is healthy movement in that process of formation. In order to see whether or not there has been growth or change will require re-surveying in two years (which is probably an adequate time frame within which to evaluate progress).
  • This is also why it is so important to take great care in how you interpret the results of the survey. While our scale of 1–5 (“almost never true of me” to “always true of me”) does give helpful feedback related to the presence or absence of an attribute of Jesus in one’s life, it is important to understand this answer within the context of where people are in their current relationship to Jesus. The Journey survey also asks a 5-level spiritual maturity question that indicates one’s present relationship with Jesus, so these values must be examined together or a specific score could be very misleading. For example, a score of 3 (“often true of me”) in having a regular prayer life could be a very healthy indicator of movement toward Jesus for a newer Christian, whereas the same score could be seen differently if coming from a person who considers their life centered on Jesus.
  • Similarly, a church scoring all 4’s and 5’s (“always” or “most of the time true”) on questions related to their beliefs in Jesus’ teachings could simply be a church with lots of mature believers, very little movement, and few “spiritual babies.” Their overall score may indicate more spiritual maturity but not more spiritual health when compared to a church filled with people who had just discovered Jesus and had much lower scores, reflecting their stage in the journey. Of course, this truth applies to individuals as well as to communities.

No Comparisons:

  • For these reasons, it is unhelpful to make comparisons between churches, or individuals, or to apply some arbitrary standard of development and maturity. All that matters is sensing the invitation of the Holy Spirit, welcoming you into a greater level of trust and obedience. Just as it is meaningless to compare a kindergarten student with another completing their post-graduate degree, so it is with comparing churches and/or individuals at completely different stages in their walk with Jesus. All that really counts is our present posture relative to him: are we turned toward him or turned away? When we are turned toward Jesus and ready to say yes to his invitation to trust him more, we can truly never be in a better place.

The Importance of Community:

  • The Jesus Journey survey that you have taken as a community is designed to explore the combination of belief, experience and behavior in order to show two things: various ways in which the character and life of Jesus has been established in the life of your community (a cause for celebration and thankfulness); and the growing edge in your journey with Jesus — possible next steps in responding to his invitation to become more like Jesus.
  • While individuals answer our Journey survey questions, we are not assuming that the Christian journey is primarily a personal one. We are not in competition with one another, and unhealthy comparison with each other must be avoided. The Bible makes it clear that we are first and foremost the people of God together. We all need each other and can’t optimally grow and change outside of the power of God’s presence within his community. In that sense, perhaps the greatest value of this stocktaking will be in discovering together where we are in our common journey of becoming like Jesus. That understanding will then empower us to be of the greatest possible benefit to one another as we all “reach toward the prize” that awaits us (Philippians 3:14).

Source: Prepare — Understanding the Jesus Journey Survey. © 2017 Jesus Journey Group. All Rights Reserved.

title: Step-by-Step to Success
html:
How Can I Best Prepare for the Jesus Journey Survey?

Please note: carefully following each step outlined below will make all the difference in ensuring that your survey experience is a successful and valuable one!

Early Preparation Tasks

  • Church pastor and leadership review the jesusjourney.life website information, particularly becoming familiar with all the material available through the dashboard:
    • Jesus Journey survey purposes and principles
    • Examples of survey questions to be asked of your people
    • Samples of Jesus Journey feedback reports for respondents and the church
  • Church leadership discussions and prayer over:
    • The needs and hopes for your church in understanding where people are in their lives with Jesus, not just on Sunday but through the week.
    • How the Jesus Journey survey can answer key questions about the spiritual needs of your congregation.
  • A possible schedule for conducting the survey and getting your results report.
  • Selecting a primary contact who will coordinate the survey process and confirm that when you register with the Journey team. This person will receive all correspondence, coordinate the survey activities within your church, and be able to download the church report and guidance for interpretation — so it will be important to choose someone who has some technical aptitude and the necessary commitment to review all of the preparatory material.

Survey Preparation Tasks

  • Meet with key church elders, deacons, and ministry leaders to discuss the survey and commit together to its purposes and to encouraging your people to participate.
  • Prepare an email announcement of the survey that will go out to your members.
  • Prepare an announcement and promotional slides (if used) for church announcements and your website. (Note: graphic templates are available in the Resources tab.)
  • Prepare short texts that can be used in church bulletins and newsletters.
  • Plan on a schedule for completing the survey. It is suggested that you take 2 weeks to prepare your congregation, then 2 weeks for people to complete the survey, with a specific date for closing the survey.
  • Decide if you will offer a paper survey option. If so, build a team to support this. (See instructions for entering paper surveys under the Collect tab.)

Survey Implementation Tasks

  • Announce the Journey survey 2 weeks before starting. Excite your people about how this will help the church, and help those who take it see where they are in their Journey with Jesus. Let people know the date when this will start and how they can take the survey (computer, tablet, smart phone).
  • Schedule the following events to occur upon completion of the survey:
    • Immediately following receipt of the survey, schedule four hours to initially review and analyze the reports that are available upon completion of the survey. A collaborative working session by the senior leader along with 1 or 2 key leaders is usually best.
    • If possible, the next day schedule another four hours with ministry staff (in a larger church) or key leaders (in a smaller church) as a helpful next step. The focus of this meeting is both summarizing the results discovered in the session above and training the staff / leaders to learn to “see” the results for themselves.
    • Within the next week, have an invitation-only meeting booked with the members / core community of your church to summarize the report results and to give ample opportunity to reflect on and give input into them.
    • On the Sunday following the members’ meeting, give a message to the whole community along the theme of our journey toward Jesus in which you present briefly the three greatest strength areas of the church and the three primary opportunities for growth.
    • In the following week or two, try to have scheduled several town hall meetings or focus groups for anyone who wishes to attend (each meeting will have the same format) wherein a summary of the report is presented and opportunity given for input and discussion. (For an example format of these meetings, see Act — Engaging the Church on the dashboard.)
    • In the weeks following the final meetings, arrange for a staff / leaders retreat where you can digest the findings generated through the various reports and interactions and direct them toward a strategic process (see Act — Making a Plan on the dashboard).
  • One week before the survey start date for the church, ask your pastors and key leaders to take the Journey survey so they know how it goes and can motivate others to take it.
  • On the Sunday when the Journey survey goes live for the church, excite people about it and encourage EVERYONE to take it. Not everyone likes to take surveys (say that!) but stress how important this is to your church, how the information will be used (not just another report that will be filed!), and that completing the survey itself will help each person better understand where they are in their journey to be more like Jesus. Let them know that each person taking the survey will get their own personal and private feedback report.
  • Make sure all your small group, Sunday School, ministry leaders and others are encouraging their people to take the survey. Some groups may want to do it together as a class or group exercise.
  • At various points throughout the survey period, check your dashboard to find out how many surveys have been completed. Use that information to encourage more participation and get higher response rates. If you are close to the end of your survey period and less than 50% of your people have responded, consider what extra steps you may take to increase participation or even consider extending your survey period. (Please note: you will not be permitted to close the survey until your survey sample size is sufficiently large to ensure valid results.)
  • After the survey closing date, thank everyone for participating. Also let them know when the report will be coming to the church and your next steps for reviewing the findings, deciding on what actions the church might take, and how the congregation will be informed of what was learned.
  • Celebrate the lessons that are learned, and the beauty of having a church growing in its many ways of journeying with Jesus.

Source: Prepare — Step-by-Step to Success. © 2017 Jesus Journey Group. All Rights Reserved.

title: Keys to Success
html:
Defining Success

  • Leaders have a good picture of where their people are on their journeys with Jesus.
  • The church itself understands the diversity of people’s walks with Jesus and how to support and encourage each other on their respective journey pathways.
  • A large percentage of the church participates in the survey so that the picture is reasonably accurate. This is extremely important if we expect the results of the survey to be reliable in the picture it presents of our community. Think through the following questions in advance: What is the size of the congregation that will be relevant to the survey? Who is to be included? Will you include your youth, only people who come on a particular Sunday, people who are visitors on that Sunday, or all the people who are on your membership or email list? That population is the total number of people who could participate. From that community (we call this “the population” in sampling language), the survey could be completed by anyone. The people who participate in the survey are the sample of the church. Ideally, the sample and the population are the same, but this almost never happens. Everything we have learned about sampling indicates that a sample of 25% or less is non-representative, and not really that trustworthy in terms of what we can learn from them. Interesting, yes; useful, not so much. A sample of 50% or more tends to be representative and trustworthy in the aggregate. There might be some people who are not represented very well, but overall the picture of the church should be quite good. So a less-than-50% response rate can get more iffy, and everything that can be done, should be done to achieve that as a minimum.
  • After review of the findings, a planning process is thoughtfully developed to encourage and grow people in the many ways they journey with Jesus.

Promotion

  • Lead pastor / team leader support is a must! This must be encouraged before, during, and after the survey. Begin to announce the survey about 2 weeks before you plan to implement.
  • Ask key leaders to support it within their groups, Sunday school classes and ministries.
  • Include links to the survey in church member emails and on website sections for members only.
  • Put Journey survey information in the Sunday bulletin.
  • Use Sunday announcements and emails to update the congregation on the value of the Journey survey and your current response rates.

Taking the Survey

  • The Journey survey can be taken by anyone who is attending the church; this includes people who are not yet fully committed to Jesus; those who are mature believers; and everyone in between.
  • The survey itself is taken online on any device with a website connection: computer, tablet, smart phone.
  • A printed version of the survey is available on the Dashboard under “Collect” for people who are visually impaired, do not have access to a device, or feel uncomfortable completing an online survey. If this option is made available, then volunteers will need to take the completed written surveys and enter the information into the website for each person (see instructions for entering paper surveys under the “Collect” tab). This will be an important segment of the congregation, so inviting volunteers to help with this could be a valuable ministry.
  • The Journey survey can be taken by anyone 16 years of age and older. Getting a picture of the spiritual needs of older adolescents and young adults can be quite important.
  • Some churches have given time during or after the church service to take the survey as part of the community. Of course, the church Wi-Fi may not be sufficient to support this in all settings. After the service may be a good time to do this for those who are completing the paper version.

Keys to Making the Information Useful

  • At least half the church must participate. That is key. The more people participate, the better and more reliable the data. Make sure they know their answers are anonymous. All reports will only report summary information, not any personal information on any one person.
  • Ask everyone to answer ALL the questions, even if they are not always completely sure of their answer.
  • Invite everyone to answer the written question at the end of the survey; it will give them a chance to tell your church leadership how you can help them on their Journey with Jesus.
  • Remind people that this will only take about 10 to 15 minutes of their time — and that they will benefit themselves from taking the survey, answering the questions, and then reflecting and praying about what they learned about their own personal Journey with Jesus.
  • Make sure they understand that each person completing the survey will get a personal feedback report on the areas of the journey with Jesus where God is already working in their lives, as well as the areas where they are being invited to grow in their walk with Jesus. They can review that report on their device, and they can save it for reading and praying over later.
  • Reporting back to the church on the key findings is necessary to validate people’s participation. Not doing this tells people that this is not important and will undermine future survey efforts.
  • Working through the findings with key leaders is critical. Answer the questions at the end of your survey report. Take seriously the guide that is provided for working through the data. Report back to the church on the steps you are taking to address any ways that will help people grow on their Journeys with Jesus.

Source: Prepare — Keys to Success. © 2017 Jesus Journey Group. All Rights Reserved.

title: Starting Our Jesus Journey Survey
html:
Step 1: Initiate with Leaders

All the Jesus Journey survey preparation work for your congregation pays off when you initiate the survey for your people. Before inviting your full congregation to participate, you should start the survey a week or so ahead for just you and your leaders to take it. Take time to pray for God’s leading in this important effort, and for his guidance in how best to invite your people to use this means to grow personally and together in your walks with Jesus.

The process is simple: go to your church Dashboard on the Jesus Journey website and push the start button on the front page. You will enter the start date for the survey, including the date when your leaders can participate, and the end date — approximately 2 weeks after your congregation is invited to participate. That will produce a URL (website link) to your own church survey. You can then distribute that URL address to your leadership team so they can take the survey, experience the questions that they will be asked, and then receive a personal report based on their answers. Your leaders are then ready to encourage others in your community to have the same experience they had.

Step 2: Initiate with the Church

You are now ready to invite your church to take the Jesus Journey survey. If you followed the plan, you and your leaders have already taken the survey, received personal feedback reports, and can testify that it was easy and helpful. You might even have one or two people talk about their experience.

You can link the survey to any newsletters you send out to your members, add the link in your church bulletin, and put it on any projections that you use in your church services. If your church website has a section for members, then you can put it there as well. This should not be open to the public at large, as that might skew the picture of your own church community.

Be sure to remind people that the Jesus Journey survey:

  • Only takes 10–15 minutes
  • Everyone 16 and older can take the survey, including those who are new to the church and those who are not yet sure of God’s place in their lives
  • Can be taken on any computer, tablet or smart phone
  • Will encourage people to reflect on the areas of their walk with Jesus that are already strong and other areas where God might be calling them to grow
  • Gives a personal feedback report on 3 of those areas where God is already moving well in their lives, as well as 3 areas where God may be inviting them to grow stronger
  • Shows that the church is taking this seriously and will reflect together on what is learned and how together we might move toward a stronger relationship with Jesus
  • Gives an opportunity at the end of the survey to offer any comments or suggestions for how we as a church can strengthen your walk with God
  • Is completely private — no one in the church will know anyone’s answers or see the feedback reports they personally receive. The church only gets a summary report from everyone who takes the survey.

Step 3: Initiate with Those Who Need a Paper Version

Consider those people in your community who may not be computer savvy or have a disability and will need to take the survey orally or on a paper version. This can be done with the Jesus Journey survey process. Doing this takes some additional work, since the paper surveys still must be entered into the online survey via a computer device. This means you will need volunteers who will take the paper surveys and enter them on a computer or other device for each of these surveys. This paper-survey process has a privacy assurance method so that people taking the survey with this method can still get a personal feedback report that only they can see.

For those who may need to take the survey orally, someone with whom they have confidence could read the questions to them, and enter the survey into a computer or device for them.

Detailed instructions for managing and entering paper surveys, and a printable copy of the Jesus Journey survey, are provided below under Paper Survey Option.

Source: Collect — Starting Our Jesus Journey Survey. © 2017 Jesus Journey Group. All Rights Reserved.

title: Journey Survey Monitoring
html:
Tools are provided on the Journey survey Dashboard for you to monitor the progress of the surveys of your church. It is very important for you to work hard to get a response rate (% of surveys completed from your church population of persons 16 years of age and older) that is at least 50%.

Overall Response Rate Monitoring

When you started the survey process, you entered a number for the people in your church who could take and would be encouraged to take the survey. That should have included everyone who comes to your services, regularly or irregularly, that is 16 years of age and older. The Dashboard uses that number for the denominator of your response rate. So if that number is 150, and 15 people have completed the surveys, then your response rate will be 10%.

Know that the number of surveys completed is key. Some people will start the survey but for some reason not continue. Those people will not be included in the response rate. A person can walk away from the survey for less than 15 minutes and come back to complete it. But it is best to take the survey at one time and finish it so that their information is used for your church report. Only those who complete the survey will receive a personal feedback report.

Subgroup Response Monitoring

Monitoring the responses of different groups of people in your church can be very helpful. The Dashboard provides you help with this by telling you how many men and women have taken the survey, as well as the numbers of people in different age groups: 16–29, 30–49, and 50 and older.

Only you know if these numbers align with the picture of your church. If you see that about half of your people are men, but men are not taking the survey, then more needs to be done to encourage them to participate. The same may be true for the age groups that make up your church.

This Dashboard monitoring tool is vitally important. Sometimes, some groups of people just don’t get the message that the Jesus Journey survey is really important to them or the church, or that their perspectives have less value than others. They may feel that this is for others, not for them. The experience of the Journey survey team thus far is that this reluctance to participate is higher for men, younger adults, and those who are less mature in their faith. All of these groups are vitally important to the church, and the Dashboard will tell you if you are getting good participation from men, women, and those from different age groups. This does not affect your response rate; it does affect the survey representativeness of your church, and your ability to understand the needs of those from key parts of your community. Note that we do not have a tool on the Dashboard to give you a picture of those who are less mature in their faith, but you are encouraged to invite them to take the survey and their vital information will be provided on your final church report.

Source: Collect — Journey Survey Monitoring. © 2017 Jesus Journey Group. All Rights Reserved.

title: Running Your Survey Reports
html:
How Do You Know You Are Ready?

You are ready to run your reports when 1) you have reached the target end date for your survey and 2) your response rate is at or above 50%. If you have been monitoring your response rates, and the actual number of responses from different groups in your church, you will know that it is time to see your reports. If your response rates are less than 50%, you should consider extending the survey time frame for another week or so and motivating your church to respond.

As an example, one larger church had reached their target date with only 33% responding, and very few of their youth and young adults participating. They extended their survey for 10 days, motivated their leadership, targeted this age group, and ultimately yielded a 55% response rate. Their reports would have provided a very poor picture of their church if they had run their reports on their target date.

Run Your Reports

This is the easy part. On your church Dashboard, push the button to create your reports. When you do so, you will receive two reports, each in PDF format for easy printing and copying:

  • A numerical and graphic Church Report that summarizes the data from the survey.
  • A Comments Report that provides the written comments to the question that your people answered on how they would like the church to help them in their walk with Jesus.

Please carefully review the text on how to understand these reports in the Interpret section of your Dashboard.

Source: Collect — Running Your Survey Reports. © 2017 Jesus Journey Group. All Rights Reserved.

title: Using the Supplemental Paper Survey
html:
Why Use a Paper Survey?

  • There may be some people in the congregation for whom using a computer, tablet, or phone to take the Journey survey is hard. These might be persons who have a physical handicap or, because of their age, are not used to entering information on a screen.
  • The paper survey may provide a way to have the survey taken by more people in the congregation, and improve your overall rate of response.

Cautions in the Use of the Paper Survey

  • Every paper survey has to be entered into the online survey system. That means you will need volunteers who can enter these paper surveys by hand, and this will take extra time.
  • You have to be sure that every person taking the paper survey answers all the questions. If any answers are left blank, then the survey cannot be entered and that person’s information is lost.
  • Every person who takes the Jesus Journey survey will receive a personal report on their walk with Jesus, their strengths, and their areas where they are being invited to grow. To keep that report private for those taking the paper survey, each person is asked at the end of the survey for a person ID that only they know. They must answer this question in order to receive this personal report. And the church must carefully follow the instructions for the paper survey to ensure that these reports are kept confidential.

Source: Collect — Using the Supplemental Paper Survey. © 2017 Jesus Journey Group. All Rights Reserved.

title: Interpreting Your Church Numerical Report
html:
Pay Attention to Sample Size

  • After the survey and report are delivered, an early examination should be given to the Church Demographics pages. First of all, is the total number in the “Church Sample Size” at least 50% of those who were invited to participate? If so, you can trust that the information in the report is quite representative of the church as a whole.
  • Second, do the numbers on those pages appear to reflect the percentages you would have expected? For example, is the % of women higher or lower than you see in the church? If so, it may mean that either men or women were less likely to respond to the survey, and may not be as well represented in the data. If the percentages are not that far off (5% difference or less), you can assume that you have reasonably good and trustworthy information from both sexes in the church.
  • The same check can be made of those from different age groups, relationship statuses, children’s ages, and ethnicities. What you are looking for are any groups that might not be as well represented in the overall report. This does not negate the value of the report, but it indicates that a church may want to get further information from that group to supplement the Jesus Journey Report, such as some small group meetings.
  • You can also look at the Jesus Journey Comments report since that will give some more detailed suggestions from some of the groups that are less well represented.
  • Note to smaller churches or groups: if the size of your community is 50–75 or lower, only the results for your entire sample can be considered reliably predictive (and only if your sample size is strongly over 50% of the entire community). The results for any subgroup (i.e. young adults or Jesus-centered people), while certainly a launch point for healthy conversation and questions, should be handled with considerable care and reservation given the unavoidably small sample size of each subgroup. While this is something to watch for even in mid-sized churches, it is of particular concern for churches or sub-groups within churches that are smaller. Note: you will be prevented from closing your survey if your sample size is too small a percentage of your overall church population — this safeguards the validity of your results. Similarly, larger churches will only be permitted to run additional sub-group reports if the sample size of a particular group is large enough to be confident of the results.

Understand Your Percentages

The numbers in the Church Report are mostly percentages. This tells us the average (or mean) number for those people who are represented in this condition. For example, if you find that 50% of the congregation is growing a lot or a little in their faith, this represents half of your people. But this does not mean this is true for everyone in the church. Other data can indicate that some people are growing much more in their faith in God than others. Who are the people growing the most, and the least? What may be behind these differences in percentages?

Numbers Are People

Numbers are just numbers; behind them are people! It can be easy to fixate on numbers. We live in a world that values numbers, some more than others. We can then start talking about numbers or percentages like they are real, when behind them are people who we care about in our congregations.

The Jesus Journey numbers represent real people who thought about the questions on the survey and responded in the best way they knew how to represent the reality of their lives at the time of the survey. Always keep that in mind. These numbers represent real people who we know and see.

What to Look for in Numbers

  • Numbers that are large tell us these are very common patterns among people. Large numbers (like 75%) can make us feel good and validate how well we are doing in our church. We can, unfortunately, focus on the “good numbers” since those validate our ministry and make us feel that what we are doing is helpful. Even as adults, we like report cards that have lots of A’s. So we can and should celebrate those numbers and search for some reasons why those numbers are high, and maybe even higher than we might have expected.
  • Numbers that are small tell us that these patterns are much less common among people. Numbers that are smaller, say 10% or 20%, may tell us even more than the large numbers that we can celebrate. A very small number of people who are not yet following Jesus may cause us to wonder if our outreach or welcoming is making it safe for people to come into our church. Another number may not be that small (say 40%) but when it represents the % of people who report that they are growing well in their faith in God, this may be of serious concern to the church. So smaller numbers can reveal a lot about our church, and where we might need to give more attention in the months and years ahead.
  • Numbers that are not expected can be the most important. Some numbers can generate a “wow” reaction: “I had no idea that…” These are numbers, and people, that deserve considerable attention and prayerful conversation. A good exercise is to ask a leadership group, before they see the report, to estimate what they think are likely to be the percent of people in the church who will answer positively some of the questions you are really curious about. There are likely to be quite a few surprises, some that we are sure will spark meaningful conversations.

Differences Between Numbers

Differences between numbers can tell us a great deal. We like to think that all is well in our community, or perhaps that more things are going well than not so well. The Jesus Journey survey is likely to reveal a lot more complexity to our church, and among our people, than we might have expected. We know there are differences in the spiritual journey of the people we see and talk to each week. But the Journey survey can reveal even more underlying patterns of beliefs, actions, and motivations than we can see each week.

You can see good examples of the differences in percentages of people on the Jesus Journey Pathways in the report. Of course these are only summary percentages, and the answers to the specific questions that yield these percentages reflect even more diversity than this. Looking at the graph of Pathways by maturity stage, we see that the complexity of the church varies even more for people who are at different levels of maturity in their journeys with Jesus. Paying attention to these differences, and knowing more about who these people are that are reflected in these numbers, is a key part of understanding the complexity of your church.

Interpreting Subgroup Numbers

Aggregate numbers and subgroup numbers can be very different. Numbers for the whole church in the aggregate can look very different from the numbers for subgroups in the church. For example, you may find that a good percent of the church considers itself Centered or Trusting in Jesus. But is that true for all subgroups in the church? Is that also true for your youth, or those new to the church, or those who are not part of a small group?

You may find that overall, a fairly high percentage of your people report that they are responding to God’s will and leading in their lives. In the aggregate that is good. But how does that look when you examine the specific questions that make up that Pathway? Are the percentages similar across the 4 questions that make up that Pathway? How different are the answers between those who see themselves as Centered on Jesus compared to those who are just coming to Believe in Jesus? To whom might you target your teachings or small group efforts that will yield the greatest growth in people’s trust in God’s leading in their lives?

Source: Interpret — Interpreting Your Church Numerical Report. © 2017 Jesus Journey Group. All Rights Reserved.

title: Interpreting Your Church Comments Report
html:
Keep Your Focus on Your People

Making sense of all the different written notes on the Jesus Journey Comments report can be more difficult than the report with lots of numbers and graphs. These comments come from people’s honest answers to the question of how they would like your church to help them walk closer to Jesus. Keep in mind that their responses to this question come after they spent thoughtful time and effort answering lots of questions that probed about their daily life with Jesus, not just on Sundays. So this is not a response to an off-the-wall question; it is likely to be heartfelt and based on all that they have been thinking about over the past 10–15 minutes when taking the Jesus Journey survey.

Use Prayerful Eyes

Be careful how you read and interpret the Jesus Journey Comments report. It is easy to scan quickly and look for the extremes — those very positive or very negative comments. Some may even be personal or can be taken personally. Instead, start by first praying for spiritual eyes to read and hear from the people in your community, many who may never have felt comfortable in another setting telling you what they are thinking or hoping. Some of these comments may sound like they are coming from the fringe, but these are the fringes that make up your church, your community. Together they tell an important story, and one that complements the more numbers-oriented Journey Survey report. They may give you insights into your priorities going forward. Listen and read with the eyes and heart of Jesus.

Examine by Differences in Spiritual Maturity

Look first for differences in comments between those at different levels of maturity in their walks with Jesus. What is each group asking for? Are there some common issues and concerns and desires among those who are Exploring Jesus, compared to those who are Believing, Trusting, or Centered in Jesus? Be careful here to look for common patterns within each category of Jesus explorers and followers. Where are they coming from? What are they hoping that the church might do to help them grow? Do they see any barriers that are limiting their abilities to draw closer to Jesus? What might be done to help them overcome those barriers?

Examine by Gender

Women and men may see the role of the church differently in helping them grow spiritually. Take a careful look just at the comments from the women, for example. Focus just on their answers. What are women’s perspectives about the church and their own desires to grow in their walks with Jesus? Are there any common themes that one can find across the comments from women? Write down these themes and see how many times each theme comes up. What patterns emerge from this? Next, do the same with the answers from men. What are they asking for, and what themes emerge from their answers? Where are the commonalities between the themes for women and men, and where are these themes different?

Examine for Key Words and Phrases

Another good comments-review strategy is to look for key words or phrases that are used across all the comments in the report. Read each comment carefully and underline or highlight words or phrases that stand out to you. For example, you might highlight “Bible study,” “families,” “children,” “youth,” “outreach,” or “pastors.” Different people might find different words that they see or consider insightful. Look for patterns in these words: how many times are some of these key words used? Are some words used more by some groups than others? What words tend to be associated with positive feelings or desires? What words are more likely to reflect less positive feelings or worries?

Examine for Generational Themes

There are also likely to be generational themes and patterns in the comments that can be explored. Not all comments can be discerned along this line, but some comments are quite likely to highlight the interests of groups such as young adults, married couples, parents, or mid-life and older adults in the church. One strategy for doing this review is to have different color highlighters that represent different generational or relational groups. Then one can read each comment, looking for those that fit a particular category of people, and highlight that comment with the appropriate color. As one reviews the overall report, then the rainbow of colors begins to reveal the patterns that each generational or relational group is concerned over and is seeking help from the church in their different walks with and toward Jesus.

Source: Interpret — Interpreting Your Church Comments Report. © 2017 Jesus Journey Group. All Rights Reserved.

title: Debriefing Preparation
html:
Preparing for the Journey Survey Debriefing Process

Senior pastor / team leader

While the survey is being conducted, there is a window in which those who give primary leadership to the community (who that is depends, of course, on the leadership philosophy and structure of your group) review the material found in the Prepare section of the dashboard to prepare themselves for the debriefing task ahead.

Immediately upon the closing of the survey period, it is important to spend up to four hours with a few key people to collaboratively work through the church report in order to analyze and interpret your results. It is a good idea to work through each page of the report as you do so, so that you fully understand how each part connects to the whole.

Reference the section on Interpreting Your Results on the Dashboard as you go through the survey, and take notes of what you discover for the next debriefing session with staff / leaders.

The format that follows is a very helpful template you can use as a structure to guide you through your report, acting as a checklist reminding you of what to look for:

  • Contents page — Begin with the contents page to summarize what is in the report. Go over key elements and principles of the Understanding the Survey section of the dashboard (perhaps produce summarized notes). Emphasize the discipline of looking first for strengths and then for opportunities for growth. Remind yourself that the results point us toward good questions to ask, not final answers that stop conversation.
  • Demographics pages — Emphasize the sample size relative to church size. Note the unique aspects of your primary demographics: what are the strengths, opportunities, and implications? Investigate the interrelationships between categories.
  • Maturity stages page — Review the 5 stages of maturity and take note that these percentages come from the second answering of the question (after respondents have answered 63 questions on where they are in their journeys with Jesus). These percentages more accurately reflect their spiritual maturity, compared to their answers to the same question at the beginning of the survey.
  • Maturity profile page — Review the maturity profile for your different groups in your church.
  • Maturity & demographics comparison pages — Apply the principles outlined in Interpreting Your Results to the comparison of maturity and demographic information. Exercise caution when the sample size of subgroups is low.
  • Spiritual change & demographics pages — Utilize the same approach to the comparison of spiritual change and demographics.
  • Pathways overview page — Explain how the three strands of belief, experience, and action are intertwined into 16 pathways.
  • Trusting Jesus goal area — Examine the results within the Trusting Jesus goal area through the lens of the 5 stages of maturity. Make note of your observations. Remember to watch for sample size, high and low numbers, and surprising or unexpected numbers and/or patterns.
  • Experiencing Jesus goal area — Examine and note results.
  • Reflecting Jesus goal area — Examine and note results.
  • Serving Jesus goal area — Examine and note results.
  • Strengths & opportunities summary page — Identify the three areas of greatest strength and the three areas with the greatest opportunity for growth.
  • Maturity comparison graph — Note the variations in the graph between Believing, Trusting, and Centered groups. Discuss the implications of the differences.

Source: Act — Debriefing Preparation. © 2017 Jesus Journey Group. All Rights Reserved.

title: Debriefing Leadership Sessions
html:
Extending the Debriefing Process — Ministry Staff

The next day, meet with ministry staff / leaders for a four-hour session that will be both informative and instructive. An example format for the meeting follows:

  • Use the format you used to debrief your results, along with the notes you took the previous day, as a template with which to guide the group through the interpretative process.
  • Begin with the contents page to summarize what is in the report. Go over key elements of the Debriefing Results section of the dashboard (perhaps give them your summarized notes). Emphasize the discipline of looking first for strengths and then for opportunities for growth.
  • Remind the group that the results point you toward good questions to ask rather than giving you final answers that will stop good conversations.
  • Start by together examining the results within the Trusting Jesus goal area. Look at these results through the lens of the 4 stages of maturity that are provided on each page of the report. Ask yourselves: what stands out as positive in what we see? Then ask: what stands out as something for us to pray and think about, where we may have some opportunities for our church to grow?
  • Next, break into three groups and have each group take one of the following sections, investigate them, and report their findings back to the whole group in terms of identified areas of strength and areas of attention for possible growth:
    • Group 1 — Experiencing Jesus
    • Group 2 — Reflecting Jesus
    • Group 3 — Serving Jesus
  • Comments Report — Introduce the Comments Report and present a summary of the results. Highlight key comments that reflect both strengths and concerns.
  • Discuss the process / timeline of the next month.
  • Plan core community / town hall meetings for the congregation.

Plan a staff retreat where you will carefully review your key results and findings and begin strategic engagement around strategies to strengthen your church.

Source: Act — Debriefing Leadership Sessions. © 2017 Jesus Journey Group. All Rights Reserved.

title: Engaging the Church
html:
Further Extending the Debriefing Process

The Process of Engaging the Church

While analyzing the data from the survey results can certainly suggest a number of conclusions, it is never safe to develop strategies and solutions based on those conclusions without reference to the actual people who took the survey.

The most productive process in debriefing this survey will involve including as many participants as possible and begin with statements like, “You seemed to say that your life with God can be characterized in this way… Let’s talk about that in order to understand what you meant and why perhaps it is that way.”

That conversation easily leads to discussing possible ways to bring change and growth. The leadership maxim that says, “people support what they create,” is especially important here.

This rich inclusion can be accomplished through two sets of meetings: one first place to start in gathering that perspective is with the core members of the community — those who are invested in the mission and values of the community. Following this meeting, you can initiate a number of town hall meetings, or alternately you could create a variety of smaller focus groups (perhaps representing the various demographic filters).

What will begin to emerge from these conversations is a shared appreciation for what has already been accomplished by the Holy Spirit — a profile of strengths — which will be invaluable in the process of growth and change. What will also begin to become clear will be those areas that appear to be the next steps of obedience and trust in following Jesus.

Members / Core Community Invitation-Only Meeting

One suggestion is to especially invite your core community members, however you define this, to review the findings of the survey first of all. In that meeting they will be introduced to what was discovered in the previous staff and leadership meetings and will be given opportunity to bring their observations and perspectives into the findings. This will broaden our understanding of what the survey report seems to tell us.

A possible outline for a Members / Core Community Meeting, from 7:00–9:00pm:

  • 45 minutes to introduce the survey and review the result summaries (distribute handout).
  • 30 minutes to break into groups and discuss: “What has been our experience of what the survey has seemed to describe to us? How do we understand what it is saying that matches with our experience?”
  • 45 minutes for reports (each successive group adds what has not yet been shared) / final summary and next steps.

Link here for sample meeting Invitation Letter. Link here for sample meeting Survey Summary Handout.

Town Hall Meetings / Focus Groups

The same format as was used for the members / core community meeting can be used for the town hall meetings.

Sunday Presentation

On the Sunday following the members / core community meeting (preceding any town hall meetings) it is helpful to give a message about the journey of following Jesus in which you have an opportunity to give to your entire congregation a summary of your three greatest areas of strength and your three primary areas of opportunity for growth. In this message you can invite people to be part of the upcoming town hall meetings to learn more and to add their insight.

Link here to Sample Message Outline (intentionally minimal in order to be personalized as much as possible) — see the Resources tab.

Source: Act — Engaging the Church. © 2017 Jesus Journey Group. All Rights Reserved.

title: Making a Plan
html:
Drawing Conclusions

As you together identify the growing edge of God’s invitation to you as a church, it will not be difficult to determine an intentional path of change. The most critical element of growth is readiness — which is the very thing that evaluation with discussion helps to nurture. Once you are aware of God’s next steps for your community (and being ready for them), determining the elements of formation and information essential to that growth is a reachable goal. Within your own church context and spheres of relationship there is generally a wealth of resources available to those who seek it out.

After you have engaged your community with a variety of inclusive conversations, what will begin to emerge are some “keys” — often-reachable initiatives that can and will have a multiplied impact. These keys only become clear with sufficiently diverse perspectives — in the midst of the differences, some common themes begin shining through.

Once the process of conversation has largely come to a close, it is essential to begin a strategic process of intentionally acting on what you have heard.

Setting 12–18 Month Goals

Your planning focus should be on a window of 12–18 months. Since there is always a lag from initial planning to effective implementation, it is a good idea to create a buffer of a few months on either side of your planning year (either calendar or school).

It is extremely important to keep staying focused on results, rather than programs. The “building” we hope to see constructed is a set of outcomes — changes in beliefs, experiences and actions. In order to do our part along with God in seeing those changes come to pass, we create programs or “intentional helping initiatives” — ways in which our staff and leaders try to help all of us reach toward God and one another toward healthy change and growth. These programmed initiatives, however, are not the real building or the end goal; they are like scaffolding on a construction site: there to enable and facilitate the actual building being completed.

Looking for Significant Strategic “Keys”

The very first thing to identify out of all the rich conversations about growth over the last weeks are the high-leverage “keys” — actions that can ultimately create a substantial difference in the overall community. (In business the question is often asked, “What is one thing that could make an 80% difference?”)

For instance, in one church we surveyed, they discovered that they had, on the one hand, a large group of mature and committed Jesus-centered people. They were actively engaged in give-and-take relationship and were by and large growing in maturity. They also had, as part of their community, a significant group of people at the beginning stages of their Jesus journey who were hungry to learn and grow. This latter group, however, was not significantly growing. The significant key they discovered was that the two groups were only connected within themselves, not to each other! What was needed to spark new growth and life was not extensive programmatic initiatives — all that was needed was to find ways to mix the two groups — something both were quite willing to do, but neither group had identified this as a problem, or a solution. This is an example of a key that has significant leverage to change things.

Three Primary Types of “Helping Initiatives”

It is helpful to think of three different types of “strands” that can help build a strong cord that can be used by people to help one another along (Ecclesiastes 4:12). Or, to use another metaphor, three elements in a soil that produces an environment conducive to growth:

  • The first is quite simply: “How can we include God more effectively into our journey of growth and change? Are there strategies, disciplines, activities that will welcome the active presence of God to be with us on our journey?”
  • The second is: “How can we more richly include our fellow pilgrims to actively journey with us, iron sharpening iron, the strong encouraging the weak? Are there relational strategies to lift us beyond simply trying to engage in a process of growth alone?”
  • The final strand or element is: “What can we gain from the wisdom resident in the larger family of God, either elsewhere beyond our local community or passed along by those who have gone before? How can we access the resources that are available but perhaps unknown to us?”

Keeping these streams of action in mind, staff and leaders can begin to identify ways in which they can help their larger community to put into intentional and consistent practice the keys that have been previously identified. In doing so, it will be important to continue to remember that these initiatives are always a means to an end and therefore will need monitoring and possible adjustment.

Working closely with their larger community, staff and leaders can construct strategies within each of the above 3 strands or soils that can in turn free up the “keys” that are needed to unlock barriers to further growth. This will involve examining existing structures / programs to determine how effectively they are encouraging and strengthening our shared journey with Jesus. It will then lead to asking, “What adjustments, additions, deletions could we enact that would more effectively partner with God’s invitation along these pathways?”

Finally, it will be necessary for the various staff and leaders holding areas of responsibility to coordinate their action plans with each other so that there is alignment through the entire system of the church. This, of course, has implications in the most practical ways for time, energy, and financial resources. In the simplest terms, this then becomes our core strategic plan.

Monitoring Progress / Adjusting Plans

If it is true, as we said previously, that programs and initiatives are the scaffolding and not the building, then it will be essential that we regularly monitor how effectively our intentional actions are encouraging the outcomes that we are hoping to see. What indicators might tell us that we are on or off track in seeing the changes that we hope to see?

It is important to schedule a focused re-evaluation approximately six months after the start of our plan and then again after the completion of the first year. That will give us opportunity to listen and to adapt.

Preparing for Survey Follow-Up

After approximately 18 months, it will be time to begin looking at repeating the Jesus Journey Survey. This will give us a comprehensive look into how our profile of strengths and opportunities has evolved. We will be able to see how the soil in which we are rooted has become more fertile and how we indeed are, as a community, growing up into Christ!

Source: Act — Making a Plan. © 2017 Jesus Journey Group. All Rights Reserved.

title: Becoming Like Jesus (Sample Message)
html:
Colossians 1:28–29 — He is the one we are proclaiming. We are instructing everybody and teaching everybody in every kind of wisdom, so that we can present everybody grown up, complete, in the king. That’s what I am working for, struggling with all his energy which is powerfully at work within me.

Why does this matter?

  • Saying yes to Jesus is the beginning of a journey toward life at its fullest, not just a contract securing the future (if just the latter, put it in a safety deposit box and grab it when you need it).
  • Eternal life has broken in to meet us / the whole point is to learn how to step toward it and embrace it — how? By trusting Jesus enough to become like him in everything (to become like Jesus is to become fully alive).
  • Not just a one-time event — saying yes to Jesus is lived out one day at a time as we learn to align ourselves with God’s “unforced rhythms of grace” (the invitations that God constantly sets before us / “will you trust me enough to live this way?”).

Is this only the concern of fathers / mothers / church leaders?

  • “That’s what I’m working so hard at day after day, year after year…” (their job to make us like Jesus?)
  • While God may give them that concern, first of all, most of all, primary concern for our spiritual journey needs to be our own. God has made it possible for us to really live, but it only can happen through an active partnership.
  • Philippians 2:12–13 — Your task now is to work at bringing about your own salvation; and naturally you’ll be taking this with utter seriousness. After all, God himself is the one who’s at work among you, who provides both the will and the energy to enable you to do what pleases him.
  • We can’t do it without God; God evidently won’t do it without us.
  • 2 Peter 1:3, 5 — Everything that goes into a life of pleasing God has been miraculously given to us by getting to know, personally and intimately, the One who invited us to God. The best invitation we ever received!… So don’t lose a minute in building on what you’ve been given (make every effort), complementing your basic faith with good character, spiritual understanding, alert discipline, passionate patience, reverent wonder, warm friendliness, and generous love, each dimension fitting into and developing the others. With these qualities active and growing in your lives, no grass will grow under your feet, no day will pass without its reward as you mature in your experience of our Master Jesus.
  • Note: is this the way we want the process of growing to be? No! We want God to do all the heavy lifting! However, every father and mother knows that if you help your child as much as they want help, they will never grow into who they need to become.

How do we do this? (Fully enter into partnership with God toward growth)

  • By daily (one day at a time) trusting Jesus to show us how to truly live, and then literally doing what he shows us.
  • Not passively but actively (constantly inviting, immersing ourselves in the story, welcoming input of others).

What happens if we say no?

  • “Unforced rhythms of grace” are always an invitation.
  • If we keep ignoring our conscience, eventually we can’t hear it.

The importance of community

  • Thank God our journey with Jesus is walked out in community (like horses on a carousel — for as many as are down, there is an equal number who are up!).
  • Hebrews 10 — don’t neglect meeting with each other / encourage each other constantly!
  • This month we began a very intentional process of finding out where we are together in this Jesus Journey and discovering how to best help one another walk in it.

Three significant strengths to celebrate

  • We believe and understand God’s big story.
  • We believe we are secure in God’s unconditional love for us and for the world.
  • We believe that God wants to be involved in every part of our lives and guide us to bring God’s goodness to the world around us.
  • These beliefs give us an anchor / foundation to plant our feet… but not to stay where we are — to be able to move ahead more fully into life and freedom.

Three opportunities to reach toward

  • We haven’t yet taken hold of what we believe is possible and actively cultivated the presence and love of God (passive, waiting for God / others to do the heavy lifting / waiting for it to happen versus reaching to take hold of it).
  • We can experience a much greater sense of God’s active leading as we love and care for others around us (let out the clutch).
  • God is inviting us to more fully step into the flow of the river of justice that flows from God’s heart (not just those who are like us).

Next steps: We can work because God is at work!

  • In coming months, exactly what we are going to do.
  • Continues this week (two meetings: where are we and what can we begin to do about it?).
  • Coming months nurturing a three-stranded cord / soils with three healthy elements:
    • How to include God more actively in our journey.
    • How to include each other more in our journey.
    • How to take full advantage of the wisdom / strength in the larger family of God.

Source: Resources — Becoming Like Jesus (Sample Message Outline). Intentionally minimal so it can be personalized for your own congregation.
